ŏcellus , i, m. dim. oculus,
I.a little eye, eyelet (mostly poet.).
I. Lit.: “blanda quies furtim vietis obrepsit ocellis,” Ov. F. 3, 19 : “ut in ocellis hilaritudo est!” Plaut. Rud. 2, 4, 8 : “turgiduli,” Cat. 3, 17 : “ebrii,” id. 43, 11 : “irati,” Ov. Am. 2, 8, 15 : “acre malum semper stillantis ocelli,” Juv. 6, 109 : “si prurit frictus ocelli angulus,” id. 6, 578 .—As a term of endearment: “ocelle mi!”
my little eye! my darling!
Plaut. Trin. 2, 1, 18 : “aureus,” id. As. 3, 3, 101 : jucundissimus meus, Aug. ap. Gell. 15, 7, 3: “cave despuas, ocelle,” Cat. 50 , 19.—So of things, like our apple of the eye: “cur ocellos Italiae, villulas meas, non vides?” Cic. Att. 16, 6, 2 : “insularum,” Cat. 31, 1 .—
II. Transf., a bulb or knob on the roots of the reed (called also oculus), Plin. 21, 4, 10, § 20.
From A Latin Dictionary (Charlton T. Lewis, Charles Short, Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1879)
